title: Mingo camps south of the Ohio
summary: “Mingo” is an outsiders’ name for Iroquois-descended families, mostly Seneca and Cayuga, who moved into the Ohio Country in the mid-1700s and acted apart from the Onondaga…
bodyMarkdown:
“Mingo” is an outsiders’ name for Iroquois-descended families, mostly Seneca and Cayuga, who moved into the Ohio Country in the mid-1700s and acted apart from the Onondaga council. In a 1992 study, A. Gwynn Henderson lists the “Mingo (Seneca-Iroquois)” with Shawnee, Cherokee, and Tutelo among mid-1700s groups in the Bluegrass and middle Ohio Valley, and says that after 1758 many of Kentucky’s Indians moved north but may have kept smaller communities and winter camps. Fort Stanwix (1768) did not ban use of the land south of the Ohio: the deed ceded it to the Crown, and the Six Nations asked that their warriors keep the liberty of hunting throughout the country. Henderson says the small southern camps were moved north as settlers arrived, and by the 1770s hunting parties had become raiding parties against the stations. When Washington reached Mingo Town on the Ohio’s west bank on October 22, 1770, he counted about twenty cabins and 70 people of the Six Nations. No Kentucky camp site is documented in these sources, so “Bluegrass camps” is a general statement, not a location.
Source: [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo)
Source: [A. Gwynn Henderson, “Dispelling the Myth: Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Indian Life in Kentucky,” Register of the Kentucky Historical Society 90, no. 1 (1992): 1–25 (PDF)](https://preservationkentucky.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Dispelling-the-Myth-17th-18th-Century-Indian-Life-in-KY.pdf)
Source: [George Washington’s diary, October 22, 1770 (Founders Online)](https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Washington/01-02-02-0005-0029)
Source: [Treaty of Fort Stanwix 1768: proceedings and deed (Oklahoma State University Library)](https://treaties.okstate.edu/treaties/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768-21783)
